title: Toldot: voice and hands (Genesis 27:22)
hookLine: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau"

lines: THE GREAT SPEECH, THE OTHER DEEDS.
cards: You know someone who says all the right things. Kind words, good values, a great speech at the wedding. Then you watch what they actually do, and it doesn't match.
Maybe you've caught yourself doing it too. Genesis has a scene built on exactly that gap. Isaac is old now, his eyes too dim to see, and he wants to give his blessing to his firstborn, Esau.
And Rebekah, who heard God say the elder would serve the younger, has a plan.

teach.b: Isaac sends Esau out hunting: bring me the food I love, and I'll bless you. Rebekah hears.
She cooks two young goats the way Isaac likes them, dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes, and covers his smooth hands and neck with goatskin, because Esau is hairy.
Jacob walks in: I am Esau, your firstborn. Isaac is suspicious. How did you find it so fast?
Jacob says God sent it his way. Now he's using God's name in the lie. Come close, Isaac says, let me feel you.
He touches the goatskin hands, and then comes the well-known line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
Isaac feels the gap: the voice and the hands don't belong to the same person. And still, he gives the blessing. The Torah doesn't hide how uncomfortable this is.

Jacob, the quiet one who dwells in tents, lies to his blind father. And the tradition notices that later, Jacob is fooled in the dark himself, by his uncle Laban, when a veiled bride turns out to be the wrong sister.
A midrash also turned the line into something else: when Jacob's voice is heard in prayer and study, the hands of Esau have no power. Both readings live side by side. One says a voice matters.
The other asks: does your voice match your hands?
Jewish ethics has a phrase for that: that your inside be like your outside.

teach.h: THE VOICE IS THE VOICE OF JACOB.
teach.b: What you say and what you do, from the same person.

how: Jewish ethics speaks of tokho k'varo, that a person's inside be like their outside, and the story of Jacob's disguise is studied each year with open discussion of what he did.

o: disguises, the goatskin on Jacob's hands
generations, a family's line through time

games.q: who did what in the tent — tap the pairs.
p: cooked the goats, planned the disguise
said, I am Esau, your firstborn
felt the hands and heard the voice

s: Isaac was completely fooled from the start
he was suspicious, felt Jacob's hands, and heard that the voice didn't match.
the tradition notices Jacob is later fooled himself
Laban gives him the wrong sister, veiled, in the dark.
the well-known line has only one traditional reading
a midrash also reads it as: when Jacob's voice is in prayer and study, Esau's hands have no power.

games.q: you're Isaac. the voice sounds like Jacob. the hands feel like Esau. what do you do?
games.why: Isaac said, the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau, and blessed him anyway.

practice: Think of one thing you say about yourself: I'm a good friend, I care about my health, family comes first. Now look at what your hands actually did this week, where voice and hands line up, and where there's a gap.
Don't beat yourself up; just choose one small place to close it.

wordCard.voice: Toldot. Generations: the portion where Jacob, in goatskin, fools his blind father, who feels a voice and hands that don't match.

carryVoice: Your line: voice and hands the same. Inside like outside. Day one hundred eighty-nine, done.

sources.q: The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.
